headline: INSTAGRAM IS OFFERING YOUTUBERS UP TO 500,000 DOLLARS TO POST THE SAME LONG FORM VIDEO THEY ALREADY PUT ON YOUTUBE, AND ITS OWN HEAD OF PRODUCT SAYS THE BRAND DEALS INSIDE THOSE VIDEOS COME ALONG FOR THE RIDE
deck: Business Insider broke the money yesterday afternoon.  Instagram has offered selected YouTubers 50,000 dollars to post their long-form videos to its new Features format, has offered others six figures, and in some cases has reached 500,000 dollars.  It is not asking for exclusivity.  Put that next to a sentence Instagram's own vice president of product gave The Hollywood Reporter on Monday, which almost nobody picked up: the advertising deals already inside those videos carry over.
tldr: Instagram has offered selected YouTubers 50,000 dollars and in some cases up to 500,000 to post their long-form videos to its new Features format the same day they go on YouTube, with no exclusivity — and its own vice president of product said on Monday that the advertising deals already inside those videos carry over.  Pull every live creator agreement this week and name same-day cross-posting explicitly, saying whether the brand integration travels with it.

Halloween advertising this year was 32 percent less likely to provoke intense fear than last year and the average measured effectiveness score moved from 5.84 to 5.85, which says the intensity dial is not the variable, while a snack brand working with a horror studio landed the ninth-scariest advert ever scored.  Next time somebody asks for a seasonal cut to be pushed harder, ask which specific thing they want more of and change only that.

Only 11 percent of connected-television advertising requests in one vendor's sample carried a usable programme name, 93 percent carried a genre label, and roughly 35 percent of those labels disagreed with the programme they were attached to.  Write a line into your next insertion order requiring the seller to report what share of delivered impressions carried a programme-level label, and treat genre targeting on free streaming inventory as approximate until they answer.

Meta disclosed that advertising run from creators' own accounts is now a 15 billion dollar annual run rate growing at 97 percent, which is the fastest-growing money anywhere near brand video and measures media spend on creator posts rather than talent fees.  Price a creator-licensed paid-media package as its own line — usage rights, platform-native shapes, fifteen to twenty testable variants — and check the usage rights on everything you delivered this quarter.

Thirty-second skippable adverts inside creator videos of 22 minutes or longer completed at 60 percent against 39 percent in videos of 8 to 12 minutes, which makes runtime an advertising decision made in an edit rather than a retention one.  Cut one version above 22 minutes on your next long-form delivery and ask the client for advertisement completion rates on both, because nobody has tested the band in between.

The only live event this week where anybody published both a peak and an average was a WNBA Finals game, where the peak sat 31 percent above the average, against about 10 percent on Sunday night football — while the biggest League of Legends world championship match was reported in peaks alone.  Contract average concurrent viewers as the measure on every live sponsorship, and discount any peak you cannot pair with an average by at least a fifth.

Pinterest missed its own guidance, said it is not happy, and named the reason: food, beverage and alcohol softened in North America while health and retail held up, and it does not expect cross-border sellers back for the holidays.  Count how much of your new-business list sits in drinks and packaged food, add health and retail targets in proportion this week, and get any live fourth-quarter number confirmed in writing rather than assumed.
